sections.title: Introduction
rules: Probability theory provides a mathematical foundation for decision making under uncertainty.
In coin tossing, the outcome heads or tails is uncertain.
A random variable represents an uncertain numeric or categorical outcome.
Probability quantifies our degree of belief in an event.
Sample spaces contain all possible elementary outcomes of an experiment.
Probability values always lie between zero and one.

sections.title: Classification
rules: In Bayesian classification, we assign an input feature vector to one of K classes.
Prior probability P(Ci) is the probability of class Ci before observing the input.
Class-conditional probability density p(x|Ci) is the likelihood of observing input x given class Ci.
Evidence p(x) sums the joint probability over all possible classes.
Bayes' rule computes the posterior probability P(Ci|x) from the prior and likelihood.
Posterior probability measures our belief in class Ci after observing input x.
Bayes' classifier chooses the class with the highest posterior probability.
Bayes' decision rule achieves the minimum probability of classification error.

sections.title: Losses and Risks
rules: In practical applications, different classification errors have different financial and operational costs.
The loss matrix specifies the penalty for choosing action alpha_i when the true class is Cj.
Expected risk measures the expected loss of taking an action given input x.
The optimal Bayesian decision minimizes the expected risk.
Zero-one loss assigns zero penalty for correct decisions and one for errors.
Under zero-one loss, minimizing risk equals maximizing the posterior probability.
A reject option allows the classifier to withhold decision when uncertainty is high.
The system rejects an input if the maximum posterior probability falls below a threshold.

sections.title: Discriminant Functions
rules: A classifier implements a set of K discriminant functions g_i(x).
The classifier chooses the class with the maximum discriminant value.
Any monotonic transformation of posterior probabilities preserves decision boundaries.
Taking the natural logarithm of Bayes' rule gives a convenient discriminant function.
The log discriminant sums the log likelihood and the log prior.
Discriminant functions partition the input space into decision regions.
Decision boundaries separate adjacent decision regions where two discriminant functions are equal.

sections.title: Utility Theory
rules: Utility theory measures the value, benefit, or satisfaction of an outcome.
Utility is the negative of loss.
Expected utility is the expected reward of choosing an action in an uncertain state.
Rational decision makers choose the action that maximizes expected utility.
Maximizing expected utility is mathematically equivalent to minimizing expected risk.

sections.title: Association Rules
rules: An association rule has the form: If X then Y.
In retail basket analysis, X is the antecedent itemset and Y is the consequent itemset.
Support measures the proportion of transactions that contain both X and Y.
Confidence measures the conditional probability that a basket contains Y given that it contains X.
Lift measures how much more often X and Y occur together than expected by chance.
A lift value greater than one indicates a positive association between itemsets.
The Apriori algorithm finds all frequent itemsets that satisfy a minimum support threshold.
The downward closure property states that all subsets of a frequent itemset must also be frequent.
Apriori prunes candidate itemsets whose subsets are not frequent.

sections.title: Notes
rules: Thomas Bayes first formulated the theorem in the eighteenth century.
Bayesian decision theory provides the optimal theoretical baseline for statistical pattern recognition.
Rakesh Agrawal and colleagues developed association rule mining and the Apriori algorithm.
